Let $h(n)$ be maximal such that in any $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$ (with no three on a line and no four on a circle) there are at least $h(n)$ many circles of different radii passing through three points. Estimate $h(n)$.

 Note that the same simple double-counting lower bound from #104 gives $h(n) \ge (n - 2)/2$. For an upper bound, I'll sketch below how to get $h(n) \le n^2\exp\left(O(\sqrt{\log{n}})\right)$. There is unfortunately still quite a large gap between these bounds.
We use the following standard projection observation. Let \(S\subset\mathbb R^D\) be finite and have no three collinear points. A generic linear projection \(\pi:S\to\mathbb R^2\) is injective and gives a planar point set with no three collinear and no four concyclic. Moreover, if two ordered triples in \(S\) have the same translation class, i.e.\[
(b-a,c-a)=(b'-a',c'-a'),
\]then their projected triples are translates of one another, and hence have the same circumradius. Thus, writing\[
\tau(S):=\#\{(b-a,c-a):a,b,c\in S\},
\]we have\[
h(n)\le \tau(S)
\]whenever \(|S|\ge n\).
Let \(B_m\) be the Euclidean unit ball in \(\mathbb R^m\), and put\[
A_{m,R}:=\mathbb Z^m\cap R B_m.
\]Define the paraboloid lift\[
S_{m,R}:=\{(x,\|x\|^2):x\in A_{m,R}\}
\subset\mathbb R^{m+1}.
\]This set has no three collinear points, since the function \(x\mapsto \|x\|^2\) is strictly convex on every affine line. Let\[
N:=|S_{m,R}|=|A_{m,R}|.
\]for \(R=\exp(\Theta(m))\), so that\[
N=R^m\operatorname{vol}(B_m)\exp(o(m)).
\]We now count translation classes of ordered triples in \(S_{m,R}\). A triple is of the form\[
(x,\|x\|^2),\qquad
(x+u,\|x+u\|^2),\qquad
(x+v,\|x+v\|^2),
\]where\[
x,x+u,x+v\in A_{m,R}.
\]Its translation class is determined by\[
u,\quad v,\quad
\Delta_u:=\|x+u\|^2-\|x\|^2,\quad
\Delta_v:=\|x+v\|^2-\|x\|^2.
\]Since all squared norms involved lie in \([0,R^2]\), each of \(\Delta_u,\Delta_v\) has only \(O(R^2)\) possible values. Thus the two lifted coordinate differences contribute \(O(R^4)\) possibilities.
It remains to count the possible base pairs \((u,v)\). Define\[
D_m:=
\{(u,v)\in\mathbb R^m\times\mathbb R^m: \exists y\in\mathbb R^m\text{ with }y,y+u,y+v\in B_m\}.
\]Then the possible integer pairs \((u,v)\) are contained in\[
\mathbb Z^{2m}\cap R D_m.
\]The body \(D_m\) is convex, contains the Euclidean unit ball in \(\mathbb R^{2m}\), and is contained in a bounded Euclidean ball. Therefore\[
|\mathbb Z^{2m}\cap R D_m|
\le
(R+O(\sqrt m))^{2m}\operatorname{vol}(D_m)
=
R^{2m}\operatorname{vol}(D_m)\exp(o(m)).
\]Letting $M = 3\sqrt{3}/2$ it's not hard to show that\[
\operatorname{vol}(D_m)
\le
\operatorname{vol}(B_m)^2 M^m\exp(o(m)).
\]It follows that\[
|\mathbb Z^{2m}\cap R D_m|
\le
R^{2m}\operatorname{vol}(B_m)^2 M^m\exp(o(m)).
\]Since\[
N=R^m\operatorname{vol}(B_m)\exp(o(m)),
\]we get\[
|\mathbb Z^{2m}\cap R D_m|
\le
N^2 M^m\exp(o(m)).
\]Including the \(O(R^4)\) possibilities for the two lifted-coordinate differences,\[
\tau(S_{m,R})
\le
N^2 M^m R^4\exp(o(m)).
\]Now choose \(m\) and \(R\) so that \(N\ge n\) and \(N=n\exp(o(m))\). Since\[
N=R^m\operatorname{vol}(B_m)\exp(o(m)),
\]we have\[
\log R
=
\frac{\log n}{m}+O(\log m).
\]Thus\[
\log\frac{h(n)}{n^2}
\le
m\log M+4\log R+o(m)
=
m\log M+\frac{4\log n}{m}+o(\sqrt{\log n}).
\]Optimizing by taking\[
m\sim 2\sqrt{\frac{\log n}{\log M}},
\]we obtain\[
\log\frac{h(n)}{n^2}
\le
4\sqrt{\log M}\sqrt{\log n}
+
o(\sqrt{\log n}).
\]as desired.
AI Acknowledgement: While the projection argument and use of paraboloid lifting to avoid collinearity was developed without AI assistance, GPT-5.5 was used to optimize the constant in the exponent and write the final comment.
